text.p: Swedish automobile maker AB Volvo on Wednesday posted a 9 percent rise in pretax profits for 1996 and reported an improvement in fourth-quarter operating income.

Volvo posted a pretax profit of 14.20 billion crowns ($1.9 billion) against market expections of a profit of 13.6 billion crowns ($1.83 billion). The results included a gain of 800 million crowns ($107.6 million) from currency operations.
Volvo sales fell to 150.06 billion crowns ($20.2 billion) compared with 171.51 billion crowns ($23.06 billion) in 1995.

The Stockholm-based company said Volvo Truck fared poorly in 1996 with sales falling 13 percent, mainly in the North American market. Volvo Bus also had weaker operating income due to increased competition and problems in South America.
Elsewhere, the company was happy with its performance.
In the fourth quarter, the auto maker posted operating profits of 1.46 billion crowns ($196 million), up from 586 million ($78.8 million) in the year-ago period.
Analysts said the fourth-quarter rise in operating profits gave a glimmer of hope the automobile manufacturer is finally breaking out of a yearlong downward trend.
"Volvo looks as if it has passed bottom," said Philip Ayton, an analyst at investment bank BZW.
"This is the first time we have a year-on-year comparison that is an improvement for two years."
While the downward trend appeared to have been broken, Volvo was cautious about being too optimistic.

Overall, the results achieved in 1996 show that much remains to be done to raise Volvo's profitability and stabilise it on a consistently high level," said Soren Gyll, Volvo's outgoing chief executive.
Volvo stock closed 1 crown (13.4 cents) lower at 179 crowns ($24.07).
